title: Anthropology optional for UPSC: papers, syllabus and preparation
seo_title: Anthropology Optional for UPSC: Syllabus and Strategy
meta_description: Anthropology optional for UPSC explained: what Paper I and Paper II cover, who it suits, how to prepare, the books to start with and how to write answers.
summary: Anthropology is one of the optional subjects in the UPSC Civil Services Main examination. It has two papers of 250 marks each. Paper I covers the foundations of anthropology, from human evolution and prehistory to kinship, religion and theory. Paper II covers Indian anthropology, including Indian prehistory, caste, village studies and tribal India.

sections.h2: How the anthropology optional is structured
paras: In the Civil Services Main examination, every candidate chooses one optional subject from the list notified by UPSC. The optional has two papers, each of 250 marks, so it carries 500 marks out of the total for the written examination. Both papers are descriptive: you write answers of fixed word lengths in a three-hour sitting.

Anthropology is popular with candidates from science, engineering and medical backgrounds as well as from the social sciences, partly because the syllabus is clearly defined and partly because it connects with general studies topics on society, tribal welfare and the Constitution. Always read the latest syllabus in the official UPSC notification before you start, since the wording is the final authority on what can be asked.
Paper I covers the discipline as a whole. In outline, it includes:
list: Meaning, scope and development of anthropology, and its relation to other disciplines. See our guide to the [branches of anthropology](branches-of-anthropology.html).
Human evolution, primates, the fossil record and the emergence of modern humans.
Human genetics, variation, race and its critique, growth and development, and demography.
Prehistoric archaeology: methods of dating and the cultures of the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic and later periods.
Culture, society, marriage, family and kinship.
Economic, political and legal organisation, and the anthropology of religion.
Anthropological theories, from evolutionism and diffusionism to functionalism, structuralism and later approaches.
Research methods, including ethnographic fieldwork, and applied anthropology.

paras: Paper II applies the subject to India. It runs from deep time to present-day policy. Broadly, it covers:
list: The evolution of Indian culture and civilisation: prehistoric, protohistoric and Indus civilisation evidence, and the fossil and archaeological record of India.
The demographic profile of India, ethnic and linguistic elements, and the contributions of Indian anthropologists.
Village studies, the caste system, its theories and changes, and the impact of religions on Indian society.
[Tribal communities of India](tribes-of-india.html): their distribution, economies, problems, constitutional safeguards and development.
Tribal administration, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, PESA, forest rights and welfare programmes.
Social change, ethnicity, regionalism and the role of anthropology in development.

paras: Anthropology suits candidates who enjoy both science and society. The biological and prehistoric parts reward students who like evolution, genetics and archaeology, while the social parts reward careful reading of ethnographies and theory. If you dislike memorising examples of particular communities or scholars, you will find Paper II demanding, because good answers depend on specific cases.

The subject also connects well with the rest of the examination. Topics such as tribal rights, the Constitution, social justice, culture and Indian heritage appear across the general studies papers and the essay. Like every optional, it requires steady preparation over several months, and no subject is an easy route through the examination.

sections.h2: How to prepare: a practical plan
paras: Start by reading the syllabus line by line and turning each line into a page heading in your notes. Then build basic understanding from a standard introductory textbook in physical anthropology and one in social anthropology, before moving to India-focused texts on prehistory, caste, village studies and tribal India. Previous years' question papers, available on the UPSC website, show the level of depth expected.

Use diagrams. Answers on human evolution, primate skeletons, kinship charts, stone tool types and the distribution of tribal communities are clearer with a quick labelled sketch or map. Learn named examples: the [Stone Age sites of India](stone-age-in-india.html) such as Attirampakkam, Bhimbetka and Burzahom; key ethnographies; and specific constitutional provisions. Write timed answers every week and get them reviewed.
list: Make one-page summaries for each theory with its main thinker, key idea, an example and a criticism.
Keep a running file of Indian case studies: communities, villages, sites and policies.
Practise drawing hand axes, cleavers, microliths and Neolithic polished axes so you can sketch them in seconds.
Link current affairs on tribal welfare and heritage to syllabus lines as you read the news.

paras: Much of the anthropology syllabus becomes easier to remember once you have seen the evidence. Handling replica tools in a [stone tools session](stone-tools-up-close.html) makes Palaeolithic and Mesolithic typology concrete. A visit to [Bhimbetka's painted shelters](bhimbetka-painted-shelters-and-prehistoric-landscapes.html) brings prehistory and rock art to life, and a guided visit to the [Bhopal Tribal Museum](bhopal-tribal-museum-material-culture-interpretation.html) gives you case studies of material culture and ritual from central India. Talaash Heritage runs these as short sessions and visits for small groups of aspirants, alongside a [prehistory field school](prehistory-field-workshop.html) for those who want a longer immersion.

faq.q: How many papers are there in the UPSC anthropology optional?
faq.a: There are two papers, each of 250 marks, for a total of 500 marks. Paper I covers the foundations of the discipline, including human evolution, prehistory, kinship, religion and theory. Paper II covers Indian anthropology, including Indian prehistory, caste, village studies, tribal India and policy.

faq.q: Can a science student take anthropology optional?
faq.a: Yes. Any graduate can choose anthropology as the optional, whatever their degree. Many candidates from science, engineering and medical backgrounds choose it because the biological and prehistoric sections draw on familiar ideas from biology. The social sections still need careful reading of ethnographies and theory.

faq.q: How long does it take to prepare anthropology optional?
faq.a: It varies with your background and the time you can give each day. Many candidates spend several months building basic understanding, followed by regular answer writing and revision. Plan to cover the full syllabus at least twice before the Main examination, with timed practice throughout.

faq.q: Which topics in anthropology optional need diagrams?
faq.a: Diagrams help in human evolution and fossil comparisons, primate anatomy, genetics, kinship charts, stone tool types, maps of prehistoric sites, and maps of tribal distribution. Simple, neat sketches with labels make answers clearer and easier to mark, but they should support the text rather than replace it.

faq.q: Is anthropology optional useful for general studies?
faq.a: Yes, there is useful overlap. Topics such as Indian society, tribal welfare, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, forest rights, culture and heritage, and social justice appear in general studies papers and the essay, and the case studies you learn for the optional can be used there too.
